subtopic_detail: Choosing the follow up test after mifepristone and misoprostol for an eight week intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 27 year old woman in her second pregnancy who has decided, after two discussions and a week to think about it, to end this pregnancy. She has one child and is clear and settled about her decision.

Her dating ultrasound shows a single intrauterine pregnancy with a crown rump length corresponding to eight weeks and one day, with cardiac activity present. She has no abdominal pain and no bleeding. Her blood group is O negative with no preformed antibodies. She lives forty minutes from the regional hospital, has her own car, and a friend has agreed to stay with her overnight.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft and non-tender, uterus not palpable abdominally, no cervical excitation, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound shows a single intrauterine gestational sac with a crown rump length of 8 weeks 1 day and cardiac activity present, blood group O negative with negative antibody screen, haemoglobin 132 g/L (115-155), chlamydia nucleic acid test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with anti-D immunoglobulin and a review in two weeks
options.rationale: This was long standing practice, but current Australian guidance no longer recommends anti-D immunoglobulin for spontaneous or induced abortion before ten weeks gestation, because the volume of foetal red cells at that gestation is below the threshold needed to cause sensitisation. Giving it exposes her to a blood product she does not need. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a low sensitivity pregnancy test in two weeks
options.rationale: The combination regimen is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and she is within that window, and confirmation of success uses a low sensitivity urine test that turns negative once the hormone falls below about 1000 IU/L, at two weeks. This avoids the false positives of a standard high sensitivity test, which remains positive for weeks after a completely successful treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Misoprostol alone repeated as needed, with a serum hCG measurement in two weeks
options.rationale: Prostaglandin alone has a complete abortion rate around eighty per cent compared with more than ninety five per cent for the sequential combination, so it is reserved for settings where the antiprogestogen is unavailable. A single hormone measurement without a baseline for comparison is also uninterpretable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Refer for surgical aspiration as her blood group makes medical treatment unsuitable
options.rationale: Being rhesus negative is not a contraindication to medical treatment, and surgical aspiration is an equally valid option chosen for patient preference, gestation beyond the approved window, or contraindications such as suspected ectopic pregnancy, an intrauterine device in place, chronic adrenal failure or long term corticosteroid use. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Mifepristone then misoprostol, with a routine pelvic ultrasound in two weeks time
options.rationale: Routine scanning after medical abortion is specifically discouraged because retained blood and debris in the cavity look abnormal on ultrasound in many women who are entirely well, and acting on that appearance leads to unnecessary surgical intervention. Scanning is reserved for continuing symptoms, heavy bleeding, or a persistently positive test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Medical abortion with sequential mifepristone and misoprostol is approved in Australia up to sixty three days of gestation and can be provided in general practice by a prescriber who has completed the required training, including by telehealth with local pathology and ultrasound. The woman needs to know that bleeding is typically heavier than a period with clots and cramping over several hours, that it usually settles over one to two weeks, and that she should present for bleeding soaking two pads an hour for two hours, fever, or severe pain not relieved by simple analgesia. Confirmation of success matters because around two to five per cent of treatments fail or leave retained tissue, and the ongoing pregnancy rate is under one per cent; the standard confirmation is a low sensitivity urine pregnancy test at two weeks or a fall in serum hormone of more than eighty per cent at one week from a pre-treatment baseline. Routine ultrasound is avoided because it detects clinically irrelevant intrauterine echoes and drives unnecessary surgery. Contraception is discussed at the same visit and can be started immediately, including insertion of an intrauterine device once the abortion is confirmed complete.
key_points: The combination regimen is approved in Australia to sixty three days of gestation
Confirm success with a low sensitivity urine test at two weeks or an eighty per cent hormone fall at one week
Routine post-treatment ultrasound drives unnecessary surgical intervention
Anti-D immunoglobulin is not required before ten weeks gestation
Contraception can be started immediately, with device insertion once completion is confirmed
explanation.pearls: A standard high sensitivity urine pregnancy test detects down to about 25 IU/L and can stay positive for four weeks or more after a completely successful medical abortion, which is why the low sensitivity test with a threshold near 1000 IU/L is used instead and why a positive standard test at two weeks causes avoidable alarm.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

subtopic_detail: A globular tender uterus with myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old administrator with three children who describes three years of periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful. She passes clots the size of fifty cent pieces and changes a super tampon and a pad hourly on her two worst days.

The pain now begins two days before the bleeding starts and continues throughout, and she has deep pain with intercourse in the week before a period. Her cervical screening test last year was negative for human papillomavirus. She has completed her family and does not want an operation if it can be avoided. On examination her uterus is uniformly enlarged to about ten weeks size, globular, mobile and tender, with no separate adnexal mass.

data_table.Examination: Uniformly enlarged globular uterus of about ten weeks size, mobile and tender on bimanual examination, no adnexal mass, no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas, cervix appears normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound shows a globular uterus with asymmetrical anterior myometrial thickening, small myometrial cysts, an indistinct endometrial to myometrial junction and no discrete fibroid; endometrial thickness 6 mm; both ovaries normal; haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155); ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation and review her bleeding in six months
options.rationale: Embolisation has reasonable results in this condition and is a genuine option, but it is a radiological intervention with a significant post-procedural pain syndrome and is reserved for women who have failed medical management. It is more established for discrete fibroids, which her scan specifically excludes. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Refer for total hysterectomy and review her in the clinic before the operation
options.rationale: Hysterectomy is the only definitive cure and is entirely appropriate for a woman who has completed her family and failed medical treatment, but she has had no medical treatment at all and has asked to avoid an operation. Offering surgery first inverts the usual ladder. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist and review her in six months
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression shrinks the uterus and stops the bleeding effectively but causes vasomotor symptoms and bone loss, so it is limited to six months without add back therapy and is generally used to prepare for surgery rather than as ongoing treatment. It is a bridging agent, not a first line one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system and review in six months
options.rationale: A globular tender uterus with asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and loss of the junctional zone on ultrasound is adenomyosis, and the intrauterine progestogen is first line because it treats both the heavy bleeding and the pain by producing endometrial and adenomyotic decidualisation and atrophy, with typical reductions in blood loss above eighty per cent. It also provides contraception and preserves the uterus, which is what she has asked for. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists

options.text: Start tranexamic acid during menses only and review her bleeding in six months
options.rationale: An antifibrinolytic reduces blood loss by roughly a third and is a useful non-hormonal option for a woman who wants to conceive or declines hormones, but it does nothing for the dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia that are half her problem here. The difference from the correct answer is that one treats both symptoms and one treats a single symptom partially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it typically presents in women in their late thirties and forties with progressively heavier and more painful periods, often with deep dyspareunia and a chronically enlarged tender uterus. Its distinguishing examination finding is a uniformly enlarged globular uterus that is tender, as opposed to the irregular firm contour of fibroids or the fixed retroverted nodular uterus of deep endometriosis. Transvaginal ultrasound has largely replaced the old idea that it can only be diagnosed after hysterectomy, and the features to look for are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, a globular shape, subendometrial echogenic lines and an interrupted or indistinct junctional zone. Iron deficiency is very common and needs treating in its own right alongside the bleeding. Treatment is stepwise: the intrauterine progestogen first, then combined hormonal or oral progestogen options, with antifibrinolytics and anti-inflammatories as adjuncts, then embolisation or ablation, and hysterectomy as the definitive cure for women who have completed their family.
key_points: A uniformly enlarged, globular, tender uterus distinguishes it from fibroids on examination
Ultrasound features include myometrial cysts and an indistinct junctional zone
The intrauterine progestogen is first line and treats both bleeding and pain
Antifibrinolytics reduce bleeding by about a third but do not help the pain
Iron deficiency accompanies it commonly and is treated in parallel
explanation.pearls: Treat the iron deficiency as a separate problem rather than assuming it will correct once the bleeding is controlled: a ferritin of 8 micrograms/L means stores are exhausted, oral iron on alternate days is better absorbed than daily dosing because of the hepcidin response, and symptoms of fatigue often improve before the haemoglobin does.

subtopic_detail: A lumbar spine T score of minus 2.6 in a woman whose periods stopped at the age of forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 47 year old librarian whose periods stopped five years ago. Two follicle stimulating hormone measurements taken a month apart at the time were both in the postmenopausal range and a chromosomal and autoimmune screen found no cause.

She declined hormone therapy at the time because she did not like the idea of taking hormones, and she has taken nothing since. Her bone density scan has now been done and is reported below. She has never fractured a bone, does not smoke, drinks two standard drinks a week, and has about one serve of dairy food a day. Her coeliac serology, thyroid function, parathyroid hormone and calcium are all normal. She has no history of thrombosis, breast cancer, liver disease or migraine with aura.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 116/72 mmHg with other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22 kg/m2, no kyphosis, height unchanged from her recorded height at age thirty, no proximal muscle weakness
data_table.Investigations: Bone mineral density T score minus 2.6 at the lumbar spine and minus 2.1 at the femoral neck, corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 48 nmol/L (50-150), parathyroid hormone and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, coeliac serology negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment for her bone density?

options.text: Start weekly alendronate with calcium and vitamin D supplementation and exercise
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates are first line for postmenopausal osteoporosis at the usual age, but in women with early menopause they are second line because they do not replace the oestrogen deficiency that is causing the loss, and long term use in a woman who may need treatment for four decades raises concerns about atypical femoral fracture. They become appropriate if oestrogen is contraindicated or declined. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

options.text: Start denosumab six monthly with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Denosumab is effective but commits the patient to indefinite six monthly injections, because stopping it causes a rebound loss of bone density with a risk of multiple vertebral fractures unless another agent is substituted immediately. That is a poor commitment to make at forty seven when a physiological alternative exists. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia

options.text: Start menopausal hormone therapy with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Menopause before forty five is treated as replacement of a hormone she should still be producing rather than as optional symptom relief, and hormone therapy is recommended until at least the average age of natural menopause around fifty one, for bone density, cardiovascular and cognitive protection. The usual risk calculus from trials in women over sixty does not apply, and she has no contraindication. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

options.text: Start raloxifene daily with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: A selective oestrogen receptor modulator increases spinal density and reduces vertebral fracture but not hip fracture, raises the risk of venous thrombosis, and causes or worsens hot flushes, which is a particular problem in a woman who is already oestrogen deficient. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia

options.text: Advise weight bearing exercise and repeat her bone density in two years
options.rationale: Exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D repletion are necessary for everyone and will be part of her plan, but as the entire treatment for established osteoporosis in a woman with five years of untreated oestrogen deficiency ahead of her, they allow avoidable further loss. Lifestyle alone is the answer for osteopenia without other risk factors. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia)
source_refs: Healthy Bones Australia

explanation.summary: Menopause before the age of forty is premature ovarian insufficiency and between forty and forty five is early menopause, and both are managed differently from menopause at the usual age. The central principle is that these women are deficient in a hormone their peers still produce, so treatment is framed as replacement until at least the average age of natural menopause, around fifty one, rather than as a short course weighed against the risks described in trials of older women. Untreated, they face accelerated bone loss with a high lifetime fracture risk, increased cardiovascular disease, and probably increased cognitive decline, which is why hormone therapy is first line for their bone protection ahead of bisphosphonates. Either standard menopausal hormone therapy or a combined oral contraceptive can be used, with the contraceptive preferred where pregnancy is still possible, which it occasionally is. Investigation at diagnosis includes karyotype, fragile X premutation testing and adrenal and thyroid autoantibodies, and bone density is measured at diagnosis and repeated every few years. Calcium intake of around 1300 mg a day and vitamin D sufficiency support whichever agent is chosen.
key_points: Menopause before forty five is replacement, not optional symptom relief
Hormone therapy is continued until at least the average age of menopause
It is first line for bone protection in this group, ahead of bisphosphonates
Stopping denosumab causes rebound bone loss and multiple vertebral fractures
Karyotype, fragile X premutation and autoantibody testing belong in the initial workup
explanation.pearls: Her vitamin D of 48 nmol/L sits just below the target of at least 50 nmol/L year round, and correcting it matters before starting any antiresorptive agent, because giving a potent bisphosphonate or denosumab to a vitamin D deficient patient can precipitate symptomatic hypocalcaemia.

subtopic_detail: Aftercare and future birth counselling on day one after theatre repair of a 3b anal sphincter injury
stem:
You are the obstetrics resident on the postnatal ward seeing a 29 year old woman on the first day after the birth of her first baby. She had a forceps birth with a mediolateral episiotomy for a prolonged second stage, and the baby weighed 3.9 kg.

The consultant repaired a tear involving more than half the thickness of the external anal sphincter in theatre under regional anaesthesia. The urinary catheter has been removed and she is voiding normally with good volumes. She has no incontinence of flatus or faeces and her pain is controlled on regular paracetamol and an anti-inflammatory. She asks what happens now and whether she will have to have a caesarean next time.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Perineal repair intact with mild bruising and no haematoma, no cellulitis or discharge, uterus well contracted at the umbilicus, lochia normal, voiding residual volume 40 mL on bladder scan
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), white cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate postnatal plan?

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives, physiotherapy and review at three months
options.rationale: Repair of an anal sphincter injury is followed by a course of broad spectrum antibiotics to reduce wound infection and breakdown, a stool softening laxative so that the first motions do not strain the repair, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with review in a dedicated clinic at around three months where continence is assessed and endoanal ultrasound and manometry are considered. That review, rather than a decision made now, determines the advice about the next birth. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Broad spectrum antibiotics and laxatives, with review only if symptoms develop
options.rationale: The immediate measures are right but waiting for symptoms misses the women who will benefit most, since occult sphincter defects and reduced squeeze pressures are common while continence is preserved in the early months and deteriorates years later. Structured follow up is what allows the next birth to be planned properly. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Laxatives and physiotherapy, with a planned caesarean section for any next birth
options.rationale: Committing her to abdominal birth on the day after the injury pre-empts the assessment that should decide it: a woman who is fully continent with normal investigations at review can be supported to birth vaginally, and elective caesarean is reserved for those who are symptomatic or have abnormal studies. Omitting antibiotics also increases wound breakdown. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Antibiotics and physiotherapy, with a constipating agent to protect the repair
options.rationale: This gets the bowel management exactly backwards. Constipating the patient produces a hard bolus that has to be passed eventually and is far more likely to disrupt the repair than soft regular motions, which is why a stool softener and not a constipating agent is prescribed. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

options.text: Physiotherapy alone, with endoanal ultrasound and manometry before discharge
options.rationale: Imaging and pressure studies belong at the specialist review months later, when oedema has resolved and the findings reflect the healed anatomy rather than acute swelling, and doing them now would be uninterpretable. Physiotherapy alone also omits the antibiotics and laxatives that protect the repair. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury

explanation.summary: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries are classified as third degree when the anal sphincter complex is involved, subdivided into less than half of the external sphincter torn, more than half torn, and involvement of the internal sphincter, and fourth degree when the anal epithelium is breached. Risk factors are a first vaginal birth, forceps delivery, a birth weight above 4 kg, a prolonged second stage, shoulder dystocia and occipitoposterior position. Repair is performed in theatre with adequate regional or general anaesthesia and good lighting, by an appropriately trained clinician, using either overlap or end to end technique for the external sphincter, with the internal sphincter repaired separately end to end when torn. Aftercare is a course of broad spectrum antibiotics, laxatives rather than constipating agents, and pelvic floor physiotherapy, with specialist review at around three months. The risk of recurrence at a subsequent vaginal birth is around five to seven per cent, and elective caesarean is offered to women who have persisting symptoms or abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, while asymptomatic women with normal studies may plan a vaginal birth.
key_points: Third degree tears are subdivided by how much of the external sphincter is torn
Antibiotics and laxatives, not constipating agents, protect the repair
Pelvic floor physiotherapy and specialist review at around three months are standard
Recurrence risk at a subsequent vaginal birth is roughly five to seven per cent
Elective caesarean is offered for persisting symptoms or abnormal investigations
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about incontinence of flatus and about faecal urgency at every review rather than about faecal incontinence alone, because loss of control of wind and an inability to defer a motion for more than a few minutes are the earliest and commonest symptoms of a sphincter defect, and women very rarely volunteer them.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists: Obstetric anal sphincter injury
Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care

subtopic_detail: Fifteen hot flushes a day in a woman taking tamoxifen after receptor positive early breast cancer
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 49 year old graphic designer fourteen months into tamoxifen, prescribed after breast conserving surgery and radiotherapy for a grade 2 oestrogen receptor positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 negative early breast cancer.

She counts fifteen to twenty hot flushes a day and wakes four times most nights drenched. She is falling asleep at her desk, has taken three days off this month, and tells you she is close to stopping the tablets because she cannot go on like this for another four years. Her mood is not low and she is enjoying her work when she is rested. She is still having periods and takes no other medication. Her oncologist has written asking you to manage the symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Surgical scar well healed with no mass in either breast, no axillary lymphadenopathy, no chest wall nodules, body mass index 24 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), full blood count and liver function within normal limits, most recent mammogram and ultrasound reported as no evidence of recurrence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for her flushes?

options.text: Start transdermal oestradiol with micronised progesterone for symptom control
options.rationale: Systemic oestrogen is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms and is contraindicated after a receptor positive breast cancer, where trial evidence showed an increase in new breast cancer events. The transdermal route changes the thrombotic risk profile but not the hormonal one. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

options.text: Start paroxetine 20 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: This class does reduce flushes, but paroxetine and fluoxetine are potent inhibitors of the enzyme that converts tamoxifen to its active metabolite, and using them together lowers that metabolite substantially with observational evidence of increased breast cancer mortality. The drug class is right and this particular member is the one to avoid. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

options.text: Stop the tamoxifen and switch to an aromatase inhibitor for the remaining years
options.rationale: Aromatase inhibitors do not work in a woman who is still menstruating unless ovarian function is suppressed, and adding ovarian suppression would deepen the oestrogen deficiency and make the flushes considerably worse. It also changes her cancer treatment without her oncologist, when the request was to manage the symptoms. (Source: Cancer Council Australia)
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia

options.text: Start a vaginal oestradiol pessary and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: Low dose vaginal oestrogen is used cautiously for genitourinary symptoms in selected women after breast cancer, but systemic absorption is minimal by design, so it has no effect on hot flushes. It answers a different symptom from the one she has presented with. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

options.text: Start venlafaxine 37.5 mg daily and review her flush frequency in four weeks
options.rationale: A serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor is the best studied non-hormonal option for vasomotor symptoms and typically reduces flush frequency by about sixty per cent, and venlafaxine is specifically preferred in women on tamoxifen because it is a weak inhibitor of the enzyme that generates the active metabolite. Treating the symptom effectively is also what protects five years of adjuvant endocrine therapy she is otherwise about to abandon. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society

explanation.summary: Vasomotor symptoms are the commonest reason women stop adjuvant endocrine therapy early, and non-adherence to tamoxifen translates directly into higher recurrence and mortality, so treating the flushes is oncological treatment rather than a comfort measure. Systemic menopausal hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer. Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen, its potent active metabolite, so strong inhibitors of that enzyme are avoided: paroxetine and fluoxetine are the ones to know, along with bupropion and quinidine, while venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine, escitalopram and citalopram are weak inhibitors and are considered safe. Effective non-hormonal options in order of evidence are the serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, gabapentin at night where sleep disturbance dominates, clonidine, and cognitive behavioural therapy or hypnosis, which have good trial evidence and no interactions at all. Vaginal oestrogen is a separate question for genitourinary symptoms and is used cautiously and usually with oncologist involvement, particularly for women on aromatase inhibitors.
key_points: Untreated flushes drive early discontinuation of endocrine therapy and worsen outcomes
Systemic hormone therapy is contraindicated after receptor positive breast cancer
Tamoxifen requires cytochrome P450 2D6 to form its active metabolite
Avoid paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion; venlafaxine and escitalopram are acceptable
Gabapentin at night and cognitive behavioural therapy are effective alternatives
explanation.pearls: If flushes at night are the dominant problem, gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime is worth knowing as an alternative to the antidepressants because it reduces night time flushes by a similar margin, has no interaction with tamoxifen at all, and its sedation is useful rather than a drawback when the symptom is waking her four times a night.
